newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr depressed, but jobs offer hope.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr depressed, but jobs offer hope.

text.p: The Australian dollar dipped into danger Thursday after surrendering another support level to fears of a domestic rate cut and an exodus of offshore funds.
The loss deepened the technical gloom engulfing the currency and left dealers happy to go short in the belief last week's 5-1/2 month low at US$0.7738 would soon be surpassed.
So sour was sentiment that evidence of unknown strength in the labour market had yet to have the impact it deserved.
"The data changes the tone of things in the economy," said Anthony Thompson, an economist at HSBC Markets. "So much so that the Reserve Bank may be prepared to wait on an easing."
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar was hovering nervously at US$0.7753/58 having retreated from US$0.7778/83 late Wednesday.
The currency had cracked US$0.7770 support offshore as investors reacted badly to a Japanese newspaper report that institutions there were shifting funds from A$ to US$ assets.
The seachange was prompted by narrowing yield differentials and intense speculation about another cut in Australian rates.

Indeed, dealers said much of the early selling was the market betting that key jobs data today would be dire enough to guarantee a policy easing. In the event not only were the figures far from weak, they held an upbeat sting in the tail.

Employment rose by a modest 4,500 in December which was down from 24,500 the month before but dead in line with market estimates of a 5,000 gain. The unemployment rate ticked up to 8.6 percent from 8.5, again much as forecast.
However, the Statistics Bureau revealed that a new method of compiling the data had had the effect of dampening reported employment growth.

The new method, introduced in August, meant average jobs growth was 6,000 to 9,000 a month lower than what would have been reported under the old system. This added up to between 30,000 and 45,000 jobs in five months.
This was a not insignificant amount considering that the reported jobs growth in the period was 58,000 and suggested the labour market was not nearly as soft as previously thought.
"As a result, it is hard to build a strong case why the employment picture might encourage the RBA to ease monetary policy again," said UBS Australia economist Stephen Roberts.

He noted that a cumulative 150 basis points of easing had still to largely impact the economy and the last cut in December had been accompanied by a 2.5 percent depreciation in the currency for an added easing of monetary conditions.
Even the money market, the fount of much rate cut rumour in recent days, had taken pause at the data and pulled the 90-day bank bill future back five basis points to 94.32.

But that still implied a rate a 5.68 percent compared to the present official cash rate of 6.00 percent, so the speculation was by no means over. Some calm might descend for a while as the next major release with a relevance to policy was not due until Janaury 29 when inflation for the December quarter are out.
On the crosses the local currency drifted to 90.63/73 yen from 90.93/03 late Wednesday and to 58.0 in trade weighted terms from 58.2. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
